analysis.one_liner: Makes personal bankruptcy harder by imposing an income test, mandatory credit counseling, and new rules favoring lenders.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: introduced January 30, 2001 with 6 cosponsors (4 Democrats, 2 Republicans), it sat on the Senate calendar for two years and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal bankruptcy law to make it harder for households to wipe out debts in Chapter 7 and push them instead into multi-year repayment plans under Chapter 13. It does this with a formula-based 'means test' that presumes abuse for debtors above median income, mandatory pre-filing credit counseling, new hurdles to discharge, and stronger rights for secured lenders. It also carries real consumer protections: child support debts jump to first priority, retirement and education savings get shielded, creditors face penalties for abusive practices, and credit card companies must disclose more to customers.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers and other unsecured lenders gain the most: debtors who would have erased their debts in Chapter 7 would instead repay them over five years under Chapter 13, and stricter reaffirmation rules would keep more obligations alive. Secured creditors (auto lenders, mortgage holders) gain new protections and faster relief from the automatic stay. Credit counseling agencies gain a mandatory role that every consumer bankruptcy filer must pass through first. Credit unions win a specific carve-out letting them reaffirm debts with lower court scrutiny. Family farmers gain permanent Chapter 12 bankruptcy protection. A smaller set of debtors also benefit: child support claimants get first priority, retirement and education savings are protected, and victims of creditor abuse can have claims cut by up to 20 percent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card issuers and unsecured lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a formula 'means test' that presumes abuse — and forces dismissal or conversion to a repayment plan — whenever a debtor's income, minus IRS-set expense allowances, exceeds set thresholds ($10,000 or the greater of $6,000/25% of unsecured claims over five years), with debtors above their state's median income most exposed [S3].

It requires every consumer debtor to complete a credit counseling briefing from a U.S.-trustee-approved nonprofit agency within 180 days before filing, and to finish a financial management course before receiving a discharge [S3].

It gives lenders faster relief from the automatic stay when a debtor fails to surrender collateral, tightens luxury-goods and repeat-filing rules, lengthens the interval between Chapter 7 discharges, and extends Chapter 13 plans to five years in more cases [S3].

It strengthens creditor-side enforcement too: debtor attorneys face cost liability and civil penalties if a trustee's dismissal motion succeeds, and the Attorney General must designate U.S. attorneys and FBI agents to pursue abusive reaffirmations and false bankruptcy schedules [S3].
The bill also reenacts Chapter 12 family-farmer bankruptcy permanently and raises its debt limit, protecting farm households whose reorganization chapter had repeatedly lapsed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households that need bankruptcy pay most: above-median-income filers lose access to Chapter 7 unless they rebut a presumption of abuse with documented 'special circumstances,' and all filers take on counseling course fees, attorney fee-risk, and disclosure burdens. Debtors' bankruptcy lawyers face new penalties and reimbursement duties that raise the cost of representation. Below-median-income debtors are carved out of most of the new restrictions, and several provisions protect ordinary filers — retirement funds and education savings are shielded, child support moves to the top repayment priority, and creditors who unreasonably refuse a workout plan can see their claim cut by 20 percent.

drawbacks.text: The means test replaces a judge's judgment of whether a debtor can actually repay with a rigid formula built on IRS expense allowances, which can leave out real costs like childcare, medical needs, or high local rents, pushing genuinely broke families into five-year repayment plans [S3].

Mandatory pre-filing credit counseling adds a fee and a delay between a family hitting crisis and getting court relief, and creates a new gatekeeping industry that every filer must pay to pass through, with only narrow waivers for emergencies [S3].

Debtors' attorneys can be ordered to reimburse trustees and pay civil penalties if a dismissal motion succeeds, raising the cost and risk of representing struggling families and potentially pushing them into filing without counsel [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for the bill, which an honest supporter would acknowledge costs something: some debtors with real repayment capacity use Chapter 7 to walk away from debts, shifting costs to creditors and to other borrowers in the form of higher rates; the bill's 'reinforced fresh start' [S3] accepts higher debtor barriers as the price of curbing that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles genuine consumer gains — first-priority child support, protected retirement savings, penalties for abusive creditor practices, richer credit card disclosures — but its central engine is the means test and counseling mandate, which shift power and money from distressed households toward lenders. The protections below the median-income line are real, but for filers above it the formula's rigidity and the new fees and penalties make bankruptcy costlier and less effective as a fresh start. Net effect: lenders gain more than debtors do. (A nearly identical bill passed and was signed into law in 2005.)

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business in its first week, the bill never got a committee markup, floor debate, or vote, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) introduced the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2001 on January 30, 2001, alongside original cosponsors Sens. Sessions (R-AL), Hatch (R-UT), and Johnson (D-SD) [S3][S5].

The Senate read the bill twice and placed it directly on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 7 on January 31, 2001 — bypassing committee — and the action record shows no referral, markup, or floor motion ever followed [S5].
Six senators cosponsored — 4 of 49 Senate Democrats and 2 of 49 Senate Republicans — bipartisan support, but the bill sat on the calendar through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2003 [S4][S1].
The bill died without either chamber voting on it, meaning the bankruptcy rules of the time remained in place for this Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households in financial distress kept the pre-reform bankruptcy rules — including a judge's ability to decide whether Chapter 7 relief was abusive — for the rest of this Congress. Credit card issuers and other lenders, who had pushed the means test for years, saw the bill stall, though a substantially similar law eventually passed in 2005.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Struggling debtors — until a similar law passed in 2005

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it onto the Senate calendar under General Orders.

against.name: Senate floor leadership

against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up from the calendar; two years on General Orders produced no floor debate or vote.

against.name: Consumer and bankruptcy-reform advocacy groups

sides.party_line_note: The record shows bipartisan sponsorship — 4 of 49 Senate Democrats and 2 of 49 Senate Republicans joined the sponsor — but no vote ever occurred, so the bill never revealed a partisan split on the floor.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test, tighter discharge rules, and attorney-liability provisions convert debts people currently erase in Chapter 7 into multi-year repayment streams for lenders. The industry had pressed for these rules for years, and a near-identical bill became law in 2005.

Mandatory pre-filing counseling makes approved nonprofit agencies the gate every bankruptcy filer must pass through — and pay — before reaching the court. The bill sets approval standards and fee limits, but it institutionalizes the industry's role and blocks filers who can't obtain counseling within narrow exception windows.

The bill gives lenders faster relief from the automatic stay when debtors fail to surrender collateral, requires five-year Chapter 13 plans in more cases, and gives secured creditors 'fair treatment' in repayment plans — meaning debtors keep paying on car and home loans longer.

The bill carves credit unions out of the presumption that a reaffirmation agreement a debtor cannot afford is an undue hardship, letting them collect on reaffirmed debts with less court scrutiny than other lenders face.
Permanent reenactment of Chapter 12 with a higher debt limit keeps a bankruptcy path designed for farm households with irregular income. The beneficiaries are the farmers themselves.
